questions.question: Which qualification is necessary for reliability of an examiner?
questions.solution_html:
• A qualified examiner must possess academic background in forensic science and specific
  • training in questioned document analysis for reliability.
  • Definition and Nature
  • Class characteristics are generic writing habits learned during initial writing instruction.
  • They represent the framework of handwriting before individual traits emerge.
  • They help the examiner narrow down possible writers to a particular population group or
  • educational system.
  • Role of Different Instruments
  • a) Light Sources (Visible, UV, and IR)
  • Various wavelengths reveal alterations invisible to the naked eye.
  • Oblique light detects indentations or surface disturbance.
  • UV light exposes fluorescent inks, erasures, and added entries.
  • IR absorption and luminescence distinguish inks of similar color but different composition.
  • b) Stereomicroscope
  • Provides three-dimensional visualization of strokes, erasures, and pen pressure.
  • Helps differentiate between original and added writings, as well as sequence of strokes
  • (whether signature written before or after printing).
  • c) ESDA (Electrostatic Detection Apparatus)
  • Detects indented writings produced when a document is placed over another during writing.
  • In a forged cheque, ESDA can reveal impressions of genuine writings or prior attempts at
  • falsification.
  • Non-destructive and preserves original evidence.
  • d) VSC (Video Spectral Comparator)
  • Employs multi-spectral imaging to examine inks, security features, watermarks, and
  • background printing.
  • Identifies chemical differences between inks through spectral response.
  • Useful in detecting substitution of amounts or payee names.
  • e) Photomicrographs
  • High-resolution photographs taken through microscopes for documentation.
  • They record microscopic evidence of tampering, fiber disturbance, or ink deposition.
  • Essential for inclusion in forensic reports and court presentation.
  • 25900408
questions.final_answer: Option Light Sources (Visible, UV, and IR)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Name one tool commonly used for the preliminary examination of a document
questions.solution_html:
• Magnifying lens Stereomicroscope (or any relevant)
  • These tools help in visual inspection to observe pen pressure, alignment, erasures, and
  • indented writings.
  • Examples of Class Characteristics
  • Slant and slope – Right or left inclination typical to a copy-book style.
  • Letter formations – Similar shapes of ‘a’, ‘g’, ‘k’, or ‘y’ found in certain cursive styles.
  • Connecting strokes – Whether letters are connected or separated in a word.
  • Pen lifts and line quality – Even, rhythmic strokes taught during schooling.
  • Spacing pattern – Uniform spacing between letters or words as practiced habitually.
  • 25900408
  • Integrated Analytical Workflow
  • Visual and light source examination – initial observation for overt changes.
  • Microscopic analysis – confirmation of surface or ink layering.
  • ESDA scanning – recovery of latent impressions.
  • VSC testing – spectral differentiation of inks and security features.
  • Photomicrographic documentation – permanent visual record supporting expert opinion.
questions.final_answer: Photomicrographic documentation – permanent visual record supporting expert opinion
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What is another term of standard writing?
questions.solution_html:
• Exemplar -Exemplar or standard writing is a known sample of handwriting used for
  • comparison.
  • Importance in Forensic Examination
  • Class traits assist in identifying the writing system used, e.g., Palmer, Zaner-Bloser, or Indian
  • regional scripts.
  • They are crucial in early stages of comparison to group writings before focusing on individual
  • traits.
  • Recognition of class traits prevents examiners from falsely attributing similarities caused by
  • common instruction rather than authorship.
  • Forensic Interpretation- Combination of results determines whether writing is genuine or
  • altered. Detects multiple ink entries, erased payee names, or forged signatures. Maintains chain of
  • custody and scientific reliability of the report.
questions.final_answer: custody and scientific reliability of the report
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Define the term ‘case law’.
questions.solution_html:
• Law established through judicial decisions- Case law forms legal precedents guiding future
  • judgments and forensic practices.
  • Distinction from Individual Characteristics
  • Individual characteristics evolve through repeated practice, physical changes, and personality.
  • While class traits identify the group, individual traits establish identity.
  • Both are evaluated together for conclusive opinion.
  • Case Relevance- In cheque fraud cases, these combined tools can expose insertion of extra
  • digits, overwritten signatures, or replacement of payee names without damaging the document.
  • (Description of each instrument – 6 Workflow integration and analysis – 4 Forensic
  • interpretation and examples – 3 Conclusion and clarity – 2)
questions.final_answer: interpretation and examples – 3 Conclusion and clarity – 2)

questions.question: What is questioned document examination?
questions.solution_html:
• Scientific analysis of documents to determine authenticity and authorship/ It involves
  • handwriting, typewriting, ink, paper, and signature analysis.
  • Forensic Application and Examples
  • In examining forged signatures, the forger often mimics class traits but fails to reproduce
  • natural individual habits.
  • Class features also assist in identifying origin of anonymous writings (e.g., regional or
  • institutional background).
  • (Definition and concept – 3 Examples with explanation – 4 Importance and distinction – 4 Forensic
  • relevance and examples – 3 Conclusion and coherence – 1)
questions.final_answer: relevance and examples – 3 Conclusion and coherence – 1)

questions.question: List out the precautions to be taken while handling questioned documents
questions.solution_html:
• Documents must be handled with utmost care to prevent contamination or alteration.
  • Examiners should use gloves or forceps, avoid folding, writing, or making marks on the
  • document. Each exhibit should be packed in a clean, labelled cover and stored in dry
  • conditions. Moisture, sunlight, and adhesives should be avoided to preserve integrity.(
  • Precautions listed (3–4 points) – (2 marks), Emphasis on preservation and legal chain – (1 mark))

questions.question: Discuss the key features in disguised writing that help examiners differentiate it from natural handwriting.
questions.solution_html:
• Disguised writing shows intentional modifications to conceal identity. Features include
  • altered slant, inconsistent size and spacing, unnatural pen lifts, tremors, irregular pressure, and
  • abnormal letter forms. Despite efforts, subconscious writing traits like rhythm and connecting
  • strokes may persist, helping experts detect disguise. (Identification of altered characteristics 2
  • marks, Mention of persistent natural features – (1 mark))
  • 25900408

questions.question: Test your ability to identify the differences between inkjet printer and laser printer impressions
questions.solution_html:
• Inkjet printers deposit liquid ink droplets forming visible dot patterns under magnification
  • often showing edge feathering on paper. Laser printers use toner powder fused to the paper by
  • heat, producing smooth, uniform, and slightly raised prints. Toner may be removable with
  • adhesive tape, while inkjet prints soak into fibers. ( Printing principle (ink vs toner) – (1 mark)
  • Physical difference (dot pattern, texture) – (1 mark), Forensic identification aspect – (1 mark))
questions.final_answer: Physical difference (dot pattern, texture) – , Forensic identification aspect – )

questions.question: Differentiate between addition and substitution in alterations with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• Addition occurs when extra words, digits, or lines are inserted after writing (e.g., adding
  • digits to cheque amount). Substitution involves replacing original text with new content, often
  • by erasure or overwriting (e.g., changing date or name). Both are detected by magnification
  • oblique lighting, and chemical analysis of inks.
  • (Definition of both – (2 marks), Example and detection – (1 mark))

questions.solution_html:

  • by observing paper surface details. ( Description of magnification – (1 mark), Detection of

questions.question: Explain different types of forgery and explain with suitable examples how they are detected in forensic examination.
questions.solution_html:
• Forgery refers to the false making or alteration of a document with intent to deceive.
  • Types include
  • Simulated (Imitated) forgery – imitation of genuine handwriting; detected by hesitation
  • tremors, inconsistent pressure.
  • Traced forgery – copying over genuine writing using carbon or tracing paper; identified by
  • slow movement, uniform thickness.
  • Freehand forgery – forged without model; lacks genuine rhythm.
  • Electronic forgery – use of scanners or digital methods to reproduce signatures.
  • Detection involves examination of pen movement, line quality, pressure pattern, and
  • microscopic analysis. Instruments like VSC and ESDA aid in confirming forgeries.
  • Definition – 1
  • Types (at least three) – 3
  • Detection methods and examples – 2
questions.final_answer: Detection methods and examples – 2

questions.question: Explain in detail the structure of a forensic report and the significance of each section.
questions.solution_html:
• A forensic report provides scientific findings and expert opinion for court.
  • Structure includes
  • Heading and case details – Name, case number, date, authority.
  • Items received – Exhibit list.
  • Purpose of examination – Question framed by the investigating officer.
  • Methodology – Scientific techniques used.
  • Observations and results – Factual findings.
  • Opinion Conclusion – Expert’s interpretation.
  • Signature and seal – Authentication of report.
  • Each section ensures clarity, transparency, and admissibility in legal proceedings.
  • Marks
  • Proper sequence of sections – 3 Significance and clarity – 3
questions.final_answer: Proper sequence of sections – 3 Significance and clarity – 3

questions.question: Describe the different types of exemplers with suitable examples.
questions.solution_html:
• Exemplars are known handwriting samples used for comparison.
  • Types
  • Collected exemplars – Naturally written prior to investigation (letters, diaries, bank slips).

  • Informal exemplars – Everyday writings collected from casual materials.
  • Collected exemplars show natural variation; requested ones are useful for specific text
  • reproduction. Both are crucial for reliable authorship determination. ( Definition – 1

questions.question: Describe how handwriting characteristics assist in identifying the author of anonymous writings.
questions.solution_html:
• Handwriting has unique features reflecting motor coordination and habitual patterns.
  • Examiners study characteristics like slant, size, alignment, spacing, connecting strokes, loops
  • pressure, and rhythm. Even in anonymous writings, subconscious traits persist. Comparison
  • with known exemplars helps identify the probable writer using scientific reasoning and
  • statistical evaluation. (Marks: List of characteristics – 3, Explanation of persistence – 2 Role
  • in identification – 1)
questions.final_answer: in identification – 1)

questions.question: Explain in detail the steps involved in performing paper chromatography in a forensic laboratory.
questions.solution_html:
• Paper chromatography separates ink or dye mixtures.
  • Steps: Sample preparation – Ink spot placed on baseline of filter paper, Solvent
  • preparation – Suitable mobile phase (e.g., water, ethanol), Development – Paper suspended
  • in solvent; capillary action separates components, Drying and visualization – Dry paper;
  • visualize spots under UV or iodine chamber, Interpretation – Calculate Rf values; compare
  • with standards. Used for ink differentiation and age determination. (Marks: Stepwise
  • procedure 4 – Application in forensics – 2)
questions.final_answer: procedure 4 – Application in forensics – 2)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Examine how secret writings are revealed using optical and chemical techniques.
questions.solution_html:
• Secret writings use invisible inks or hidden impressions.
  • Optical methods: UV light reveals fluorescent inks. IR photography detects carbon-based or
  • heat-sensitive inks.
  • Chemical methods: Iodine fumes, ninhydrin, or lemon juice reveal writings through color
  • change.
  • Other techniques: Oblique lighting and VSC help detect indentations or pressure marks
  • Used in espionage and fraud detection. Marks: Optical techniques – 3, Chemical techniques
  • – 2 Application – 1
questions.final_answer: – 2 Application – 1
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Describe the examination process of a paper? / Part D Essay Type Questions
questions.solution_html:
• Paper examination identifies origin, type, and authenticity. Process includes: Physical
  • examination – Size, color, texture, thickness, opacity. Optical examination – Watermarks, UV
  • fluorescence, surface coating. Chemical analysis – Cellulose, fillers, coatings, pH tests.
  • Instrumental analysis – IR spectroscopy or SEM for fiber content. Paper comparison assists in
  • linking questioned and standard documents. (Marks: Steps explained – 4)
questions.final_answer: linking questioned and standard documents. (Marks: Steps explained – 4)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss class characteristics of handwriting with examples?
questions.solution_html:
• Class characteristics in handwriting are those general features that are common to a group of
  • writers who share a similar system of writing—such as people taught the same copy-book
  • style, or trained in the same regional or institutional method. These features are not unique to
  • an individual but reflect a common pattern of formation and design.
questions.final_answer: an individual but reflect a common pattern of formation and design

questions.question: Examine the role of magnification in detecting erasures during preliminary examination of documents.
questions.solution_html:
• Magnification reveals disturbances in paper fibers, abrasions, and trace residues left after
  • erasure. Under magnified view, erased regions appear rough, discolored, or uneven in texture.

questions.question: Explain different types of forgery and explain with suitable examples how they are detected in forensic examination.
questions.solution_html:
• Forgery refers to the false making or alteration of a document with intent to deceive.
  • Types include
  • Simulated (Imitated) forgery – imitation of genuine handwriting; detected by hesitation
  • tremors, inconsistent pressure.
  • Traced forgery – copying over genuine writing using carbon or tracing paper; identified by
  • slow movement, uniform thickness.
  • Freehand forgery – forged without model; lacks genuine rhythm.
  • Electronic forgery – use of scanners or digital methods to reproduce signatures.
  • Detection involves examination of pen movement, line quality, pressure pattern, and
  • microscopic analysis. Instruments like VSC and ESDA aid in confirming forgeries.
  • Definition – 1
  • Types (at least three) – 3
  • Detection methods and examples – 2
questions.final_answer: Detection methods and examples – 2

questions.question: Explain in detail the structure of a forensic report and the significance of each section.
questions.solution_html:
• A forensic report provides scientific findings and expert opinion for court.
  • Structure includes
  • Heading and case details – Name, case number, date, authority.
  • Items received – Exhibit list.
  • Purpose of examination – Question framed by the investigating officer.
  • Methodology – Scientific techniques used.
  • Observations and results – Factual findings.
  • Opinion Conclusion – Expert’s interpretation.
  • Signature and seal – Authentication of report.
  • Each section ensures clarity, transparency, and admissibility in legal proceedings.

  • Informal exemplars – Everyday writings collected from casual materials.

questions.question: Examine how secret writings are revealed using optical and chemical techniques.
questions.solution_html:
• Secret writings use invisible inks or hidden impressions.
  • Optical methods: UV light reveals fluorescent inks. IR photography detects carbon-based or
  • heat-sensitive inks.
  • Chemical methods: Iodine fumes, ninhydrin, or lemon juice reveal writings through color
  • change.
  • Other techniques: Oblique lighting and VSC help detect indentations or pressure marks

questions.question: Discuss class characteristics of handwriting with examples?
questions.solution_html:
• Class characteristics in handwriting are those general features that are common to a group of
  • writers who share a similar system of writing—such as people taught the same copy-book
  • style, or trained in the same regional or institutional method. These features are not unique to
  • an individual but reflect a common pattern of formation and design.
